The cost of a small abstraction

9 November · six minutes

There is a particular kind of abstraction that feels free when you write it and costs you every week afterwards. It is small, it is plausible, and it hides a decision you will later want to revisit.

The shape of the problem

You have three call sites that do almost the same thing. Almost. A helper appears, the differences become a parameter, and the parameter becomes an enum.

Six months later the enum has eleven values, one of which is unused but cannot be removed because nobody remembers what it protected.

A test that would have helped

Before writing the helper, ask whether the three call sites change for the same reason. If they change for different reasons, they are not one thing.

Duplication is cheaper than a wrong boundary, because duplication is visible.

What I do now

I write the second copy without comment and wait for the third. By the third, the boundary is usually obvious, and if it is not, I have learned something about the problem.

The exception is a boundary that holds a secret or an invariant. Those I draw early, because the cost of getting them wrong is not measured in lines of code.

None of this is new. It is just easy to forget when the helper takes five minutes to write.

The sidebar carries navigation and advertising, which should never be translated as content.
